clues: It has the longest coastline of any country.
It has the world’s largest area of freshwater lakes.
It shares the longest international land border in the world.
It’s the second-largest country by area, and its capital is Ottawa.
fact: Its lakes are why it ranks only fourth by land area despite being second by total area. Its border with its southern neighbour is the longest land border on Earth.

clues: It is made up of 14,125 islands.
Its highest mountain is an active volcano that last erupted in 1707.
That mountain is Mount Fuji, 3,776 metres tall.
Its capital is Tokyo.
fact: Kongō Gumi, a temple-building company founded here in 578, built and repaired shrines and temples for more than 1,400 years. Mount Fuji became a World Heritage Site in 2013.

clues: It’s the only NATO member with no standing army.
The English word “geyser” comes from a hot spring here.
Its parliament, the Althing, dates back to around 930.
About 35% of its roughly 395,000 people live in its capital, Reykjavík.
fact: Geysir is the oldest known geyser in the world. Its parliament has a claim to being one of the longest-running in the world.

clues: More than half its people live on one island, the most heavily populated island on Earth.
It’s the world’s largest archipelagic state, with between 13,000 and 17,000 islands.
It has the largest Muslim population of any country.
Its capital is Jakarta.
fact: Java holds more than half of its people. Islam is followed by about 87% of the population.

clues: It’s the most sparsely populated sovereign state in the world.
About 30% of its people are nomadic or semi-nomadic.
Its capital is the coldest capital city in the world.
Genghis Khan founded an empire here in 1206. It’s landlocked between Russia and China.
fact: Ulaanbaatar averages −1.3 °C over the year, colder than any other capital.

clues: In 1893 it became the first nation to give all women the vote.
Its national icon is a flightless bird.
That bird is the kiwi.
Its capital is Wellington.
fact: Bats were its only known native land mammals until a fossil find in 2006. With no mammal predators, several of its birds lost the power of flight, the kiwi among them.

clues: It has been named the happiest country in the world nine years in a row.
It has over 180,000 recorded lakes.
Nokia started here in 1865, as a pulp mill.
Its capital is Helsinki.
fact: It also hosts the Wife Carrying World Championships, held in Sonkajärvi since 1996.

clues: Over 90% of its wildlife is found nowhere else on Earth.
It grows about 42% of the world’s vanilla.
Lemurs live naturally here and nowhere else.
It’s the world’s fourth-largest island, off the south-east coast of Africa.
fact: Millions of years of isolation let its plants and animals evolve on their own. In 2023 it produced 42% of the world’s vanilla.

clues: The Nazca culture flourished on its coast.
The largest empire in the pre-Columbian Americas ruled from a city here.
Machu Picchu is here.
Its capital is Lima.
fact: The Inca built the largest empire in the pre-Columbian Americas, with Cusco as its capital. Machu Picchu is the citadel that became its icon.

clues: It claims about 1.25 million km² of Antarctica.
Easter Island has belonged to it since 1888.
Its Atacama Desert was the site of the 2010 San José mine collapse.
Its capital is Santiago.
fact: It also administers the Juan Fernández Islands in the Pacific. Its Antarctic claim is called the Chilean Antarctic Territory.

clues: The world’s largest coral reef system, over 2,300 km long, lies off its coast.
It has the longest fence in the world: 5,614 km, built to keep dingoes out.
In 1932 its army fought a “war” against emus, and abandoned it.
Its capital is Canberra.
fact: Soldiers with machine guns spent five weeks in the Emu War in 1932. The emus scattered into small groups and the cull was called off.

clues: It has the largest Portuguese-speaking population in the world.
It’s the fifth-largest country on Earth by area.
It borders every other country on its continent except Ecuador and Chile.
Its capital is Brasília.
fact: It ranks first among the world’s 17 “megadiverse” countries, and borders nine countries plus one French territory.

clues: Officially it has no capital at all, just a “federal city”.
It has four language regions: German, French, Italian and Romansh.
It’s the birthplace of the Red Cross.
It has been neutral since the 16th century, and hasn’t fought an international war since 1815.
fact: Bern is the seat of government but not, legally, the capital. Its neutrality was recognised by Europe’s powers in 1648.

clues: Along with Liberia, it’s the only African country never fully colonised.
It hosts the headquarters of the African Union Commission.
It’s the second most populous country in Africa, and has no coastline.
Its capital is Addis Ababa.
fact: Italy occupied it from 1936 to 1941 but never secured the whole country. Around 138 million people live there.

clues: It lifted its ban on television and the internet only in 1999.
Its national anthem is called “The Thunder Dragon Kingdom”.
About 71% of it is forest, and it famously measures Gross National Happiness.
It’s a Himalayan kingdom between China and India. Its capital is Thimphu.
fact: It was one of the last countries in the world to introduce television. Its name in its own language means “Land of the Thunder Dragon”.

clues: The Louvre, the world’s most-visited museum, stands in its capital.
The Eiffel Tower was built as the centrepiece of its 1889 World’s Fair.
It borders Belgium, Germany, Italy and Spain, and its overseas regions include French Guiana.
Its capital is Paris.
fact: The Eiffel Tower was completed on 31 March 1889 and is 330 metres tall to its tip. The Louvre had 9.0 million visitors in 2025.

clues: The Great Pyramid, built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2600 BC, stands here.
It spans two continents: the northeast corner of Africa and, via the Sinai, the southwest corner of Asia.
It is the most populous country in the Arab world, with over 107 million people.
Its capital is Cairo.
fact: The Great Pyramid stood 146.6 metres tall when it was built. It’s about 138.5 metres today, because its limestone casing was removed.

clues: Its 1791 constitution was described as Europe’s first modern one.
Its statehood is traced to a ruler’s conversion to Christianity in 966.
The Solidarity movement, credited with helping start the fall of the Iron Curtain, began here.
Its capital is Warsaw, and it borders Germany to the west.
fact: The state began forming under the Piast dynasty, after the ruler of a tribe called the Polans converted to Christianity in 966.

clues: It declared independence as a “First Republic” on 11 July 1811.
Angel Falls, the world’s tallest uninterrupted waterfall at 979 metres, plunges here.
Its name means “Little Venice”, inspired by stilt houses on Lake Maracaibo.
It has the world’s largest known oil reserves, and its capital is Caracas.
fact: Angel Falls is named after Jimmie Angel, an American aviator who flew over it in 1933. Its Pemon name, Kerepakupai Merú, means “waterfall of the deepest place”.

clues: It was the last Soviet republic to declare independence, in 1991.
In the early 1500s its khanate stretched across the steppes east of the Caspian Sea and north of the Aral Sea.
It is the ninth-largest country in the world, and the largest landlocked one.
Its capital is Astana, and it borders Russia to the north and China to the east.
fact: Almaty, its largest city, was the capital until 1997.

clues: Yellowstone, widely understood to be the world’s first national park, was established here in 1872.
The Statue of Liberty, a gift from the people of France, was dedicated here in 1886.
It consists of 50 states and a federal capital district, and borders Canada and Mexico.
Its capital is Washington, D.C.
fact: Its economy has been the world’s largest since about 1890.

clues: The Taj Mahal, a white marble mausoleum, stands in Agra.
It is the world’s most populous country, and the seventh-largest by area.
It shares land borders with Pakistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Myanmar.
Its capital is New Delhi.
fact: Shah Jahan commissioned the Taj Mahal in 1631 as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. The wider complex was complete by 1653, and UNESCO listed it in 1983.

clues: Its name comes from the surname of the Italian navigator Christopher Columbus.
It is one of the world’s seventeen megadiverse countries, with Amazon rainforest and Andean highlands.
It has coasts on both the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean, and declared independence from Spain in 1810.
Its capital is Bogotá.
fact: Simón Bolívar finally proclaimed its independence in 1819.

clues: It became independent on 21 March 1990, though Walvis Bay stayed under South African control until 1994.
It is the driest country in sub-Saharan Africa.
It takes its name from the Namib, the oldest desert in the world.
Its capital is Windhoek, and it was a German colony from 1884.
fact: Before independence it was called German South West Africa.

clues: It was the first Soviet republic to break away, restoring independence on 11 March 1990.
In the 14th century its Grand Duchy was the largest country in Europe.
In 1569 it merged into a Commonwealth with Poland.
Its capital is Vilnius, on the eastern shore of the Baltic Sea.
fact: A sand peninsula called the Curonian Spit shelters much of its Baltic coast.

clues: Two independent microstates are surrounded by it: San Marino and Vatican City.
It has more UNESCO World Heritage Sites than any other country: 62.
The Colosseum, built in AD 70–80 for gladiatorial contests, stands in its capital.
Its capital is Rome, on a peninsula that extends into the Mediterranean Sea.
fact: The Colosseum held an estimated 50,000 to 80,000 spectators, around 65,000 on average.

clues: Millions of wildebeest and zebra cross the Mara River here in the Great Migration.
Africa’s second-highest mountain, just south of the equator, gave the country its name.
Its official languages are Swahili and English.
Its capital is Nairobi.
fact: That mountain’s highest peak, Batian, is 5,199 metres tall. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997.

clues: It was never colonised, acting as a buffer between Imperial China and British India.
Lumbini, the Buddha’s birthplace according to Buddhist traditions, is here.
It has eight of the world’s ten highest mountains, including Everest.
Its capital is Kathmandu, and it is landlocked between China and India.
fact: On 28 May 2008 it was declared a federal republic, ending its Hindu monarchy.

clues: Silver from the mines of Potosí once made up over half of the world’s output.
It lost its Pacific coastline to Chile in 1879.
It has two capitals: Sucre, the constitutional capital, and La Paz, the seat of government.
It is named after Simón Bolívar, and is landlocked in central South America.
fact: Its Salar de Uyuni, at 10,582 square kilometres, is the world’s largest salt flat, and holds most of Bolivia’s lithium, about 22% of the world’s known reserves.

clues: Its king is elected to a five-year term by and from among nine hereditary rulers.
The South China Sea splits it into two regions, one of them on the island of Borneo.
The Petronas Towers, once the world’s tallest buildings, rise in its capital.
Its capital is Kuala Lumpur, and it became independent on 31 August 1957.
fact: The Petronas Towers are 451.9 metres tall and remain the world’s tallest twin towers. A double-decker skybridge links them on the 41st and 42nd floors.

clues: The Maya pyramid El Castillo, at Chichén Itzá, is one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.
Sixty-eight indigenous languages are co-official here alongside Spanish.
It borders the United States to the north and Guatemala and Belize to the southeast.
Its capital and largest city bears the country’s own name.
fact: El Castillo is about 30 metres high, and Chichén Itzá became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988.

clues: IKEA, founded here in 1943 by Ingvar Kamprad, is the world’s largest furniture retailer.
The Nobel Prize ceremonies, except the Peace Prize, are held in its capital on 10 December.
It is the largest and most populous Nordic country, bordering Norway and Finland.
Its capital is Stockholm.
fact: Alfred Nobel, the Swedish chemist and inventor who created the prizes in his will, died on 10 December, the date of the ceremonies.

clues: In November 1989 the Velvet Revolution ended communist rule here.
It is traditionally made up of Bohemia and Moravia, with Silesia in the northeast.
Czechoslovakia peacefully dissolved at the end of 1992, making it independent on 1 January 1993.
It is landlocked, bordered by Austria, Germany, Poland and Slovakia, and its capital is Prague.
fact: Its capital was the imperial seat in 1346–1437 and 1583–1611, and the 1618 Defenestration of Prague began the Bohemian Revolt.

clues: The Sahara covers most of it, except the fertile and mountainous north.
It is the tenth-largest country in the world.
It gained independence in 1962, after a war against France that began in 1954.
Its capital is Algiers, on the Mediterranean coast.
fact: Most of its people live in the northern strip between the Mediterranean Sea and the desert.

clues: It seceded from Colombia in 1903, with American backing.
It sits on a narrow isthmus between two oceans, linking North and South America.
A canal completed in 1914 connects the Atlantic and Pacific here, and was handed over on 31 December 1999.
Its capital, home to nearly half its people, shares the country’s name.
fact: The 1977 treaties agreed to transfer the canal from the United States to Panama on 31 December 1999.

clues: Oktoberfest, the world’s largest Volksfest, draws around seven million visitors to Munich each year.
It is the most populous member state of the European Union.
East and West were reunited on 3 October 1990.
Its capital is Berlin, and it has nine neighbours.
fact: The first Oktoberfest was held on 12 October 1810, to celebrate the wedding of Crown Prince Ludwig and Princess Therese.

clues: Its former name was Siam.
It was the only country in Southeast Asia to avoid colonisation by European powers.
It is a constitutional monarchy bordering Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia and Malaysia, with a coast on the Andaman Sea.
Its capital is Bangkok.
fact: It became a parliamentary constitutional monarchy after 1932.

clues: The Ngorongoro Crater, the world’s largest inactive and intact volcanic caldera, is here.
It was formed in 1964, when Zanzibar merged with Tanganyika.
Africa’s highest mountain, Kilimanjaro at about 5,895 metres, rises here.
Its capital is Dodoma, though the former capital, Dar es Salaam, keeps most government offices.
fact: Lake Victoria, Africa’s largest lake, lies to its north and west, and Lake Tanganyika, the continent’s deepest, to its west.

clues: Its independence day, 24 May 1822, marks Sucre’s victory at the Battle of Pichincha.
The Galápagos Islands lie about 1,000 kilometres west of its mainland.
It is one of 17 megadiverse countries, and the US dollar is its only official currency.
Its name is Spanish for “Equator”, and its capital is Quito.
fact: The summit of its volcano Chimborazo is widely reported as the point on Earth’s surface farthest from the Earth’s centre, because of the equatorial bulge.

clues: Moldavia and Wallachia united in 1859 to form its modern state.
Its name comes from the Latin “romanus”, meaning citizen of Rome.
It lies on the northwestern shore of the Black Sea and borders Ukraine to the north and east and Hungary to the west.
Its capital is Bucharest, and Transylvania was granted to it by the Treaty of Trianon in 1920.
fact: Transylvania and other former Hungarian territories went to the Kingdom of Romania under the Treaty of Trianon.

clues: In Buñol, thousands of people throw tomatoes at each other at La Tomatina, on the last Wednesday of August.
Antoni Gaudí’s Sagrada Família, begun in 1882, is still under construction here.
It covers the majority of the Iberian Peninsula, and includes the Balearic and Canary Islands.
Its capital is Madrid.
fact: La Tomatina began in 1945, and attendance is capped at 20,000 ticket holders. In 2015 an estimated 145 tonnes of tomatoes were thrown.

clues: It has three capital cities: Pretoria, Cape Town and Bloemfontein.
It completely encloses another country, Lesotho.
It has twelve official languages.
It sits at the southern tip of Africa, and Cape Town is its legislative capital.
fact: Pretoria is the administrative capital, Cape Town the legislative one and Bloemfontein the judicial one.

clues: The explorer Ferdinand Magellan arrived in 1521 and claimed the islands for Spain.
It was named in honour of King Philip II.
It is an archipelago of about 7,641 islands in the Pacific Ring of Fire, prone to earthquakes and typhoons.
Its islands fall into three groups, Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao, and its capital is Manila.
fact: Manila is the capital, but the largest city is Quezon City.

clues: It is one of only two doubly landlocked countries in the world, the other being Liechtenstein.
It is the only Central Asian state to border all four of the others.
Bukhara and Samarkand grew extremely wealthy on Silk Road trade.
Timur, or Tamerlane, rose here in the 1380s, and its capital is Tashkent.
fact: The Aral Sea, on its border, was once the fourth-largest inland sea on Earth and has since shrunk to about 10% of its former area.

clues: It became independent on 30 September 1966, having been the British-ruled Bechuanaland.
It produces more diamonds than any other country except Russia.
About 70% of its territory is part of the Kalahari Desert.
Its capital is Gaborone, and it is landlocked in Southern Africa.
fact: Its Okavango River spreads across the Kalahari in a large inland delta instead of reaching the sea.

clues: A system of fortifications over 21,000 kilometres long, the Great Wall, runs across its north.
Giant pandas, which are about 99% bamboo-eaters, are found naturally nowhere else.
It is the world’s second-most populous country, and the third largest by area.
Its capital is Beijing.
fact: The first walls date to the 7th century BC. The best-known sections were built in the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), and UNESCO listed the Wall in 1987.

clues: The Parthenon, a temple to Athena begun in 447 BC, stands on its Acropolis.
It is often considered the cradle of Western civilisation and the birthplace of democracy.
It has thousands of islands, with up to 227 of them inhabited.
Its capital is Athens, and it borders Albania, North Macedonia, Bulgaria and Turkey.
fact: The Parthenon was completed in 438 BC, with its decoration continuing until 432 BC.

clues: It declared perpetual neutrality in 1955, after Allied occupation.
It was the heartland of the Habsburg monarchy from the late 13th century.
It is a landlocked country in the Eastern Alps, bordering Germany, Italy, Switzerland and more.
Its capital is Vienna, which is also its largest city.
fact: The Compromise of 1867 created the dual monarchy of Austria-Hungary.

clues: It permanently abolished its army, having abolished its military force on 1 December 1948.
It never fought for independence from Spain, and celebrates it on 15 September 1821.
Its name means “rich coast” in Spanish, and it has 14 known volcanoes.
Its capital is San José, and it borders Nicaragua and Panama, with coasts on the Caribbean and the Pacific.
fact: It is one of the countries with the greatest biodiversity in all of Latin America.

clues: It became an independent sovereign country in 1965.
Its modern era began in 1819.
It has the second-highest population density of any country, spread over one main island and more than 60 satellite islets.
This island city-state sits off the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula.
fact: It is both an island country and a city-state.

clues: Big Ben, the bell in the Elizabeth Tower, hangs beside its Houses of Parliament.
It was the first industrialised country in the world, in the 18th century.
Stonehenge, a prehistoric monument of upright stones begun around 3100 BC, stands here.
Its capital is London, and its head of state is a monarch.
fact: The Palace of Westminster, where the House of Commons and House of Lords meet, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.

clues: Aconcagua, the highest mountain outside Asia, rises in its Mendoza Province.
It is the second-largest country in South America, and the eighth-largest in the world.
It shares the bulk of the Southern Cone with Chile to the west.
Its capital is Buenos Aires.
fact: Aconcagua is about 6,960 metres tall, the highest peak in the Americas.

clues: Its name comes from the river that runs through the country.
More than 250 ethnic groups speaking 500 distinct languages live here.
It gained full independence from the United Kingdom on 1 October 1960.
It is Africa’s most populous country, and its capital is Abuja, not its largest city, Lagos.
fact: It lies between the Sahel and the Gulf of Guinea, with over 242 million people.

clues: It was commonly known as Persia in the Western world until 1935.
Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Empire here, described as the largest-ever Iranian state.
The Caspian Sea lies to its north.
Its capital is Tehran, and a 1979 revolution overthrew its monarchy.
fact: Middle Paleolithic sites are found mainly in its Zagros Mountains.

clues: The “Singing Revolution” of 1988–1990 protested against Soviet rule here.
It has over 2,300 islands and islets, including Saaremaa and Hiiumaa.
It declared independence on 24 February 1918, and restored full independence on 20 August 1991.
It faces Finland across the Gulf of Finland, and its capital is Tallinn.
fact: Latvia lies to its south and Russia to its east.

clues: It is the largest country in the world, spanning eleven time zones.
Lake Baikal, the world’s deepest lake at 1,642 metres, is in its Siberia.
It shares land borders with fourteen countries.
Its capital is Moscow.
fact: Lake Baikal is also the world’s oldest lake, at roughly 25–30 million years, and holds about 23,600 cubic kilometres of fresh water.

clues: Usain Bolt, who set world records of 9.58 seconds for 100 metres and 19.19 for 200 in 2009, was born here.
It is the third-largest island in the Greater Antilles and the Caribbean.
It gained independence from the United Kingdom on 6 August 1962.
Its capital is Kingston, and its tallest mountain is Blue Mountain Peak.
fact: Its original name, Xaymaca, is glossed as “Land of Wood and Water”. England took the island from Spain in 1655.

clues: It declared independence from Yugoslavia in 1991.
Its Adriatic coast is dotted with over 1,000 islands and islets.
It borders Slovenia to the northwest and Hungary to the northeast.
Its capital is Zagreb, and it uses the euro.
fact: The word “cravat” comes from Croatian mercenaries who served in France in the Thirty Years’ War, and whose knotted neckerchiefs caught Paris’s eye.

clues: It is an absolute monarchy ruled by a sultan.
Its Musandam region is bounded by the Strait of Hormuz.
It lies in the southeastern Arabian Peninsula, sharing land borders with Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen.
Its capital and largest city is Muscat.
fact: The Banu Nabhan controlled the frankincense trade on the overland route through Sohar.

clues: It owes its name to the river that forms its northern and eastern border.
It nearly surrounds The Gambia.
It is the westernmost country of mainland West Africa.
Its capital and largest city is Dakar.
fact: France gained control of Gorée, a minor hub of the Atlantic slave trade, in 1677.

clues: Its largest city, Istanbul, is not its capital.
Anatolia makes up most of it, with a smaller part called East Thrace in Southeast Europe.
It borders Greece and Bulgaria in the west, and Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan and Iran in the east.
Its capital is Ankara.
fact: Ankara is its second-largest city.

clues: 26% of the country lies below sea level.
Rotterdam, the busiest port in Europe, is here.
Its capital is only nominal: the government sits in The Hague.
Its capital is Amsterdam, and it borders Germany and Belgium.
fact: “Holland” is really just two of its twelve provinces, North and South Holland. Its Golden Age made it one of the world’s richest trading nations.

clues: It was formerly known as Ceylon, and gained independence in 1948.
It is separated from India by the Gulf of Mannar and the Palk Strait.
After coffee plantations were destroyed by disease, the British began cultivating tea instead.
Its largest city is Colombo, while Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte is its legislative capital.
fact: Buddhism arrived from India under King Devanampiya Tissa.

clues: It was the first country in the world to fully legalise cannabis.
It is the second-smallest sovereign nation in South America, after Suriname.
It secured its independence between 1811 and 1828.
It lies between Argentina and Brazil on the Río de la Plata, and its capital is Montevideo.
fact: Its capital is home to nearly 2 million of its roughly 3.5 million people.

clues: It is often called “Africa in miniature”.
It became a German colony in 1884, known as Kamerun.
Its highest point, at almost 4,100 metres, is a mountain that bears its name.
Its official languages are French and English, and its capital is Yaoundé.
fact: French Cameroun became independent on 1 January 1960, and the British-administered south joined in 1961.

clues: Its pop culture wave, including K-pop, has become globally influential.
Its alphabet, Hangul, was created by Sejong the Great to promote literacy.
It occupies the southern half of its peninsula, bordering its neighbour along the Demilitarized Zone.
Its capital is Seoul.
fact: About half its population lives in the Seoul metropolitan area.

clues: It is the largest country in the Caribbean by area.
It lies south of both Florida and the Bahamas.
It remained part of the Spanish Empire until the Spanish–American War of 1898.
Its capital is Havana, and a revolution overthrew its government in January 1959.
fact: It includes the main island plus 4,195 other islands, islets and cays.

clues: Its language is among the few in Europe outside the Indo-European family.
It became a Christian kingdom under King Stephen I in the year 1000.
A revolution failed here in 1956.
It is landlocked in Central Europe, and its capital is Budapest.
fact: It lies in the Danube’s drainage basin, dominated by great lowland plains.

clues: It is the most linguistically diverse country in the world, with about 840 known languages.
It was granted independence as a Commonwealth realm in 1975.
It makes up the eastern half of an island that is the world’s second-largest.
Its capital is Port Moresby, and the Kokoda Track campaign was fought here in 1942.
fact: The Torres Strait Islands to its south were annexed by Queensland in 1878.

clues: It restored its independence in 2006, after its union with Montenegro was dissolved.
By the mid-16th century the Ottoman Empire had annexed all of its territory.
It is landlocked in Southeastern and Central Europe, bordered by Hungary and Romania.
Its capital, Belgrade, is also its largest city.
fact: It borders eight countries.

clues: Its coast has nearly 1,200 fjords, which stretch its coastline to about 29,000 kilometres.
It runs the world’s largest sovereign wealth fund.
Svalbard, an Arctic archipelago, belongs to it.
Its capital is Oslo, where the Nobel Peace Prize is awarded.
fact: Sognefjord, at about 226 kilometres, is its longest fjord and the fifth-longest in the world. It is also about 1,308 metres deep.

clues: Vasco da Gama, who reached India by sea in 1498, was one of its explorers.
It includes the Atlantic archipelagos of Madeira and the Azores.
Its borders have barely changed since the Treaty of Alcañices in 1297.
Its capital is Lisbon, on the southwestern Iberian Peninsula.
fact: Lisbon is also its largest city.

clues: The Khmer Empire was the largest Southeast Asian empire during the 12th century.
It was a French protectorate from 1863, and gained independence in 1953.
Southeast Asia’s largest lake, Tonlé Sap, meets the Mekong here.
Its capital is Phnom Penh, and it is a constitutional monarchy.
fact: It is bordered by Thailand, Laos and Vietnam.

clues: It became a sovereign nation on 16 December 1971, after a nine-month liberation war.
It lies on the Ganges Delta, the largest river delta in the world.
It is home to the world’s largest mangrove forest.
Its capital is Dhaka, and it shares land borders with India to the north, west and east.
fact: It is one of the most densely populated countries on Earth.

clues: It was Northern Rhodesia until 24 October 1964.
Copper is its principal export.
David Livingstone named the Victoria Falls, on its southern border, in 1855.
Its capital is Lusaka, and it has eight neighbouring countries.
fact: Victoria Falls is 1,708 metres wide. Its local name, Mosi-oa-Tunya, means “the smoke that thunders”.

clues: It was the first nation to recognise the United States as independent, in 1777.
It has coastlines on both the Mediterranean Sea and the Atlantic Ocean.
The Alawi dynasty has ruled it since 1631.
Its capital is Rabat, and Casablanca is its largest city.
fact: It regained its independence in 1956 under Sultan Mohammed V, and its Idrisid dynasty dates to 788.

clues: It achieved independence in 939, after a millennium of Chinese domination.
It lies along the Gulf of Thailand to the southwest and the South China Sea to the east.
It is the world’s 16th-most populous country.
Its capital is Hanoi, and its largest city is Ho Chi Minh City.
fact: It is bordered by China to the north, and Laos and Cambodia to the west.

clues: It became independent in 1830, after a revolution.
Its capital hosts NATO’s headquarters and many other international organisations.
It has Dutch-speaking, French-speaking and German-speaking communities.
Its capital is Brussels.
fact: It is a parliamentary constitutional monarchy, bordered by the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg and France.

clues: It is historically known as the “Pearl of Africa”.
It shares Lake Victoria with Kenya and Tanzania.
Mount Stanley, in the Rwenzori Mountains, is its highest peak.
Its capital is Kampala, and it gained independence from the United Kingdom on 9 October 1962.
fact: It is landlocked in East Africa.

clues: Its first empire was recognised by treaty with the Byzantine Empire in 681 AD.
The Cyrillic alphabet was developed in its early capital, Preslav.
The Thracians are one of the three main ancestral groups of its people.
Its capital is Sofia, and it joined the European Union in 2007.
fact: The Black Sea coast is its lowest point. It borders Romania, Serbia, North Macedonia, Greece and Turkey.

clues: Mecca and Medina, the two holiest cities in Islam, are here.
It occupies the bulk of the Arabian Peninsula.
It is the world’s second-largest oil producer.
Its capital is Riyadh, and it was founded in 1932 by King Abdulaziz.
